repos.title: LlamaFactory: Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
LlamaFactory is a unified framework integrating efficient fine-tuning methods to adapt over 100 large language models without custom code. It comprises three modules: a Model Loader attaching adapters like LoRA, QLoRA, and GaLore; a Data Worker standardizing dataset formats; and a Trainer supporting pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, and DPO. A key feature is model-sharing RLHF, which uses dynamic adapter switching to run the full pipeline on a single pre-trained model. The web interface LlamaBoard allows users to configure experiments and monitor training in real time.

The authors validate the framework on an NVIDIA A100 GPU using Gemma-2B, Llama2-7B, and Llama2-13B. On a corpus of roughly 400K tokens from PubMed abstracts, 4-bit QLoRA reduces peak memory to 5.21 GB for Gemma-2B compared to 17.06 GB for full tuning, while LoRA achieves a throughput of 3521 tokens/s. In downstream text generation tasks with 2,000 training examples, LoRA and QLoRA generally match or exceed full-tuning ROUGE scores across eight instruction-tuned models. Limitations include the requirement for adapter-based methods when using quantized weights and the fact that full-tuning Llama2-13B exceeds the 40GB memory limit of the test hardware.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly, so LlamaFactory unifies efficient fine-tuning methods in one framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing fine-tuning frameworks support fewer efficient methods than LlamaFactory, as its feature comparison shows.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques
digest_headlines.headline: The paper groups efficient fine-tuning into optimization methods, such as LoRA, and computation methods, such as flash attention.

digest_headlines.heading: LlamaFactory Framework
digest_headlines.headline: LlamaFactory has three modules, Model Loader, Data Worker and Trainer, with a web interface called LlamaBoard.

digest_headlines.heading: Empirical Study
digest_headlines.headline: Across tested models, quantized low-rank adaptation used the least memory and low-rank adaptation scored best on most generation tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Future work targets more modalities, parallel training strategies and stronger methods for conversational models.

digest_headlines.heading: Broader Impact and Responsible Use
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the framework to benefit open-source communities, and require users to follow model licenses.

repos.title: OpenVoice: Versatile Instant Voice Cloning
repos.paper_summary: OpenVoice is an instant voice cloning system that copies a speaker's tone color from a short reference clip while separately controlling emotion, accent, rhythm, pauses, intonation, and language. It splits the task into a base speaker TTS model (a modified VITS that takes style and language embeddings) and a feed-forward tone color converter. The converter uses an encoder, an invertible normalizing flow conditioned on a tone color vector, and HiFi-GAN decoding. The flow is trained with a KL loss against IPA phoneme features, which removes tone color from the content representation; the reference tone color is then inserted by running the flow in reverse. The base model was trained on about 30K sentences from four speakers, and the converter on 300K samples from 20K speakers. The paper reports no quantitative comparison against baselines; evaluation is qualitative, with audio on a demo site. Speed is 12× real-time on one A10G GPU (85 ms per second of speech). Cross-lingual cloning to unseen languages works when a base speaker exists for the target language. Limitations: emotion can be slightly neutralized in some cases, and the estimated 40× real-time upper bound is not yet reached.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Instant voice cloning needs a short reference clip, but existing methods lack style control and multi-language cloning without large multi-speaker data.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVoice decouples a base speaker text-to-speech model for style and language from a tone color converter that adds the reference voice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: OpenVoice is evaluated qualitatively rather than against baselines, reaching 12 times real-time speed on one graphics processing unit.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Decoupling tone color from style and language is presented as the core principle, with code and weights released.

repos.title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
repos.paper_summary: HairDeck generates the stylized hair cards of a character and the spring-bone chains that animate them, from a point cloud or a single image. Each card is one continuous token from a card VAE, and a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding denoises all card tokens of a hairstyle together with flow matching; an existence flag on each token sets the card count. A second set DiT generates the spring-bone chains from the card tokens. Training uses 36,440 CHARM hairstyles from VRoid characters, plus synthetic style augmentation and renders restyled by an image-editing model. On CHARM's 100-hairstyle test set, Chamfer distance drops from 0.0117 (CHARM) to 0.0066 and orientation error from 40.0° to 16.8°, at 1.01 s per hairstyle against 33.7 s for CHARM. On 76 rendered single-image test characters, CD is 0.0089 against 0.0139 to 0.0186 for baselines, with a 3.5% failure rate against 13.2% to 34.2%. The paper states that very short hair and alpha-textured realistic cards are outside the training data, and that no textures are generated.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing generators do not output the artist-placed hair cards of stylized characters, so HairDeck generates each card as one token.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers strand hair, realistic cards, stylized characters and set generation, but CHARM is the only prior stylized card generator.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each card is encoded as one continuous token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all tokens together without positional embedding.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On CHARM's test set HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance from 0.0117 to 0.0066 and orientation error from 40.0° to 16.8°, taking 1.01 s.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: HairDeck outputs card geometry without textures and learns only from stylized VRoid hairstyles, so short hair and realistic cards fall outside it.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation settings, appearance augmentation, chain metrics, export, baseline details, and additional comparisons and results.

repos.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
repos.paper_summary: Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting is a zero-shot prompting strategy for large language models that instructs the model to devise a plan dividing a task into subtasks before executing them. The extended variant, PS+, adds instructions to extract relevant variables and calculate intermediate results. On ten datasets covering arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning using GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT by an average of 6.3% on arithmetic tasks, reaching 76.7% accuracy compared to 70.4%. It also exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought on five of six arithmetic benchmarks. Error analysis on GSM8K shows PS+ reduces calculation errors from 7% to 5% and missing-step errors from 12% to 7%, though semantic misunderstanding errors remain at 27%. The paper notes two limitations: prompt sensitivity requires careful manual design, and the method does not address semantic understanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot chain-of-thought errors are split into calculation, missing-step, and semantic errors, and a plan-based prompt targets two of them.

digest_headlines.heading: Plan-and-Solve Prompting
digest_headlines.headline: Plan-and-Solve prompting uses a zero-shot trigger that asks the model to devise and carry out a plan, followed by an answer-extraction prompt.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use ten benchmarks with text-davinci-003 and compare against zero-shot and few-shot baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT on all arithmetic datasets and averages 76.7 against 77.6 for Manual-CoT.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places Plan-and-Solve among chain-of-thought methods that use zero-shot prompting and planning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that plan-based zero-shot prompting outperforms Zero-shot-CoT and matches few-shot CoT on some arithmetic datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Prompt design is labour-intensive and the method does not address semantic misunderstanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics
digest_headlines.headline: The paper lists the datasets and their licences and states that the prompts contain no personal information or discriminatory wording.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists trigger-sentence ablations for every dataset and example outputs from Zero-shot-PS+.

repos.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
repos.paper_summary: SWE-bench is an evaluation benchmark of 2294 software engineering tasks drawn from GitHub issues and their merged pull requests across 12 popular Python repositories. A model receives an issue text and a codebase snapshot and must produce a patch that makes the repository's fail-to-pass tests pass without breaking existing tests. Tasks were collected with a 33-stage pipeline that filters PRs for issue resolution, test changes, and successful execution. The authors also release SWE-bench Lite, a 300-instance subset, a training set (SWE-bench-train, about 19,000 instances from 37 other repositories), and two fine-tuned CodeLlama-Python models, SWE-Llama 7b and 13b, trained with LoRA on attention weights. Context is selected with BM25 retrieval or with oracle files from the reference patch. The best model, Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval, resolves 1.96% of tasks; with oracle retrieval it resolves 4.8%. Performance falls as context length grows. The authors note that the benchmark covers only Python, and that execution-based tests do not capture code efficiency, readability, or comprehensiveness.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks are saturated, so the authors propose SWE-bench, which draws tasks from real GitHub issues.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench pairs GitHub issues with merged pull requests and grades patches by running the repository's tests.

digest_headlines.heading: SWE-Llama: Fine-tuning CodeLlama for SWE-bench
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning CodeLlama-Python on issue-patch pairs produces SWE-Llama, open models that edit repositories.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Each model gets context from sparse retrieval or from oracle files that the reference patch edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Claude 2 is the best model at 1.96% resolved, and resolution falls as the total context length grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier benchmarks use narrow tasks or single functions, which SWE-bench extends to multi-file repository edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include Python-only tasks, simple baselines, and execution tests that miss readability and efficiency.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics Statement
digest_headlines.headline: SWE-bench uses public repositories with licenses permitting software use, and involves no human subjects or GitHub user data.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The source code, all 2294 task instances, and technical details for collection and evaluation are provided for reproduction.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers construction, field definitions, execution-based validation, dataset statistics, and case studies of model patches.

repos.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
repos.paper_summary:
Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) is a sparse attention layer for ultra-long context. It clusters keys in a learned latent space, and each query scores cluster centroids instead of every key. Keys are pooled four to one, grouped into buckets by Ward's agglomerative clustering, and queries pick top buckets (flat search) or descend a tree with beam search (Tree, which is subquadratic in prefill). Attention then runs over sink, window, and selected keys. Distilled-LSA (D-LSA) adds LSA to a frozen pre-trained model by training only small per-layer projections and a temperature against the frozen layer's attention. Native-LSA (N-LSA) is trained on next-token loss alone.

Evaluation uses RULER and PaperTrail, a long-context scientific reading benchmark the authors built. At 10M tokens, one D-LSA attention layer prefills 22.7× and decodes 4.6× faster than sparse attention on GLM-5.3-Flash, and 72.4× and 42.5× faster than full attention on Qwen-3.8-27B, with similar accuracy. N-LSA matches full-attention accuracy with a 1.6× per-layer training speedup at 128k tokens.

Limitations: the KV cache still grows linearly with context, tree search loses accuracy faster than flat search past 1M tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash, and N-LSA was tested only at about 0.5B parameters with flat search.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse attention indexers that score every key dominate cost at ultra-long context, so LSA clusters keys instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Sparse Attention
digest_headlines.headline: At 10M tokens the indexer takes 98% of sparse attention's prefill time, and current indexers still scan every key.

digest_headlines.heading: Latent Sparse Attention (LSA)
digest_headlines.headline: LSA clusters keys in a learned latent space, and each query scores only bucket centroids, flat or as a tree.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: D-LSA keeps accuracy close to baselines up to 10M tokens, and N-LSA matches full-attention validation loss at 128k.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Tree search loses accuracy faster than flat past 1M tokens, and native training was tested only at small scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LSA offers a practical route to ultra-long context attention, through distillation of pre-trained models or native training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers oracle key-budget tests, method symbols, training data, PaperTrail, evaluation setup, and parallelism details.

repos.title: LoongSage: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
repos.paper_summary:
LoongSage is an agent-native reinforcement learning framework for LLM post-training, built on Megatron for training and SGLang for inference, with about 14K lines of core code. Its AgentFlow layer serves agents through a Chat Completions interface and stores trajectories at the token level (Token-In, Token-Out), so sampled and trained sequences match. Black-box agents with context compaction or subagents are stored as a segment tree, and only mainline segments are trained. Three sliding-window policies bound staleness in fully asynchronous mode: no-window, window-gated (staleness at most S steps), and windowed-fifo (collection limited to one batch). TransferMesh selects a weight-transfer transport per receiver topology, such as CUDA IPC for colocated GPUs or NCCL for distributed nodes. A Teacher Manager supports multi-teacher on-policy distillation with sampled-token, top-K, full-vocabulary, and JSD estimators.

The evidence is four complete training runs, reported as steady task-reward improvement, a controlled train–inference gap, and reduced idle time. The paper does not provide a theorem. Its limitations include multi-agent credit assignment, which is left as non-trainable placeholders, and support for proprietary agent APIs, which is still under development.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RL frameworks add overhead for agentic training, so the paper proposes LoongSage, built on Megatron and SGLang.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work argues that existing RL frameworks lack explicit support for agentic trajectories, resource sharing, and rollout–optimization boundaries.

digest_headlines.heading: The LoongSage Framework
digest_headlines.headline: The architecture uses one controller over Ray actors, token-level internal interfaces, and seven planes, with three of four placement combinations supported.

digest_headlines.heading: Key Features
digest_headlines.headline: AgentFlow stores white-box and black-box agent trajectories as token arrays and segment trees, and three sliding-window policies bound asynchronous staleness.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Four training runs show rising rewards with bounded train–inference gaps, and asynchronous execution gives a 1.35× speedup.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion lists six contributions and plans to add Proximal Policy Optimization, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Low-Rank Adaptation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists author names and operational notes on hard failures, silent corruptions, and current implementation boundaries.

repos.title: SkillOpt: Executive Strategy for Self-Evolving Agent Skills
repos.paper_summary: SkillOpt is a text-space optimizer that trains one agent skill document, a natural-language procedure added to the context of a frozen target model. A separate frontier optimizer model reads scored rollouts from a training split and proposes add, delete, or replace edits. A candidate skill is kept only if it raises the score on a held-out selection split. Stability controls include a cap on edits per step (the "textual learning rate"), a buffer of rejected edits passed to later reflection calls, and an epoch-wise slow/meta update. The paper reports results on six benchmarks, seven target models, and three execution modes (direct chat, Codex, Claude Code). For GPT–5.5 in direct chat, the average gain over no skill is +23.5 points, and the average margin over the strongest per-cell baseline is +5.4 points. Exported skills are 300–2,000 tokens, built from 11–44 accepted edits. The paper also reports transfer across model scales and harnesses, and to Omni-MATH. Limitations: the method optimizes one skill for one domain, and it depends on a separate frontier optimizer model. The provided text ends before the slow/meta update is described, so that component and its ablation results are not covered here.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: SkillOpt optimizes an agent's skill document as external state, with validation-gated edits and no weight updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior skill work mainly builds or evolves skill libraries, while prompt optimizers target prompts rather than a persistent skill.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each step edits the skill with bounded add, delete and replace operations, accepted only if held-out selection score strictly improves.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SkillOpt is best or tied on all 52 evaluated cells, lifting GPT–5.5 by 23.5 points in direct chat.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Compact skills optimized this way transfer across model scales, harnesses and a nearby benchmark without weight updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists the optimizer prompt contracts, limitations, and experimental protocol with patch and split details.

repos.title: Deep Photo Style Transfer
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces a deep-learning method for photographic style transfer that preserves the photorealism of the input image while accurately matching the color and texture of a reference style image. The approach extends the Neural Style algorithm by adding two constraints to the optimization objective. First, a photorealism regularization term ensures the transformation from input to output is locally affine in color space, preventing spatial distortions like wiggly edges. This term uses the Matting Laplacian matrix derived from the input image. Second, an augmented style loss incorporates semantic segmentation masks for both images, restricting style transfer between semantically equivalent regions (e.g., sky to sky) to prevent "spillover" artifacts. The method uses a pre-trained VGG-19 network, with content features from `conv4_2` and style features from layers `conv1_1` through `conv5_1`. Optimization runs in 3–5 minutes on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU. In user studies, the method produced photorealistic results comparable to global histogram transfer methods, but achieved higher style faithfulness than Reinhard et al., Pitié et al., and Photoshop Match Color in over 80% of comparisons. Limitations include failure cases under extreme semantic mismatch between input and reference, which require manual segmentation masks to resolve.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Photographic style transfer must avoid painting-like distortion while keeping the reference style faithful.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method adds a locally affine color regularizer and semantic segmentation masks to Neural Style optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation Details
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation uses a pretrained convolutional network, two-stage optimization and merged segmentation classes.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Comparison
digest_headlines.headline: Compared with Neural Style, patch-based and global transfer methods, the approach avoids distortion and was judged most faithful more than 80% of the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The approach transfers reference style faithfully across time of day, weather, season and artistic edits while keeping outputs photorealistic.
